RID STEP 1 — PRE-COMMITMENT  
Identification strategy:  A difference-in-differences / event-study design that exploits the quasi-random assignment of “loser” (management-chosen offer) versus “winner” (union-chosen offer) outcomes in New Jersey police final-offer arbitration (FOA).  Because the arbitrator must pick one of two final offers and cases that proceed to FOA are typically balanced, the loser indicator is as-good-as-random conditional on fixed effects.  By comparing within-department changes in performance during the three years after the award to the three years before, relative to departments whose unions won, we obtain a causal estimate of the impact of a disappointing wage outcome on police effort.  

Directional hypothesis (H1):  Departments whose unions LOSE arbitration will experience a decline in performance—specifically (i) lower crime-clearance rates and (ii) fewer arrests—during the three years following the decision, relative to departments whose unions WIN.

I will not revise this strategy or hypothesis after this step.



RID STEP 2 — SPECIFICATION DISCIPLINE  
Exactly five specifications are pre-committed; no others will be run.

Notation  
• d indexes police departments; t indexes calendar year.  
• Loser_d = 1 if the arbitration outcome for department d selected management’s offer; 0 otherwise.  
• RelativeYear_{d,t} = t − AwardYear_d ∈ {-3,…,+3}.  
• Post_{d,t} = 1[RelativeYear ≥ 0 & ≤ 3]; 0 otherwise.  
• α_d = department fixed effects; γ_t = calendar-year fixed effects.  
• λ_d·t = department-specific linear time trend.  
• Y_{d,t} is the outcome.

Specification 1 (Baseline-Clearance)  
Y = clearance rate.  
Y_{d,t} = α_d + γ_t + β₁ (Loser_d × Post_{d,t}) + ε_{d,t}.

Specification 2 (Baseline-Arrests)  
Y = ln(1 + total arrests).  
Y_{d,t} = α_d + γ_t + β₂ (Loser_d × Post_{d,t}) + ε_{d,t}.

Specification 3 (Trend-Robust-Clearance)  
Same as Spec 1 but adds λ_d·t.  
Y_{d,t} = α_d + γ_t + λ_d·t + β₃ (Loser_d × Post_{d,t}) + ε_{d,t}.

Specification 4 (Event-Study-Clearance)  
Y = clearance rate; include year-relative dummies.  
Y_{d,t} = α_d + γ_t + Σ_{k=-3,k≠-1}^{+3} β₄k (Loser_d × 1[RelativeYear = k]) + ε_{d,t}.  
(Omit k = -1 to form the reference period.)

Specification 5 (Event-Study-Arrests)  
Same as Spec 4 with Y = ln(1 + total arrests).

Standard errors: Clustered at the department level in all specifications.



RID STEP 3 — FALSIFICATION GATE  
I will reject H1 if ANY of the following occur for either outcome:

1. Sign reversal: β̂ ≥ 0 in Specs 1–3 or post-award coefficients ≥ 0 in Specs 4–5.  
2. Statistical insignificance: β̂ < 0 but p-value > 0.10 (two-sided) in Specs 1–3.  
3. Failed pre-trend test: In Specs 4–5, a joint F-test that the two pre-award coefficients (k = -3,-2) equal zero rejects at p < 0.10.  
4. Insufficient post-award window (fewer than 90 % of expected obs.) — unlikely but listed for completeness.



RID STEP 4 — R CODE (self-contained)

```r
# ================================================================
#  NJ Police FOA – Wage Loss and Performance
#  Self-contained R script implementing the 5 pre-committed specs
# ================================================================

# 0. Packages -----------------------------------------------------
required <- c("data.table", "fixest", "lmtest", "sandwich")
lapply(required, require, character.only = TRUE)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------
# Expect a CSV with one row per dept-year from 1975-1999 inclusive.
# Key variables:
#   dept_id, year, award_year, loser (0/1), clearance_rate, arrests
dt <- fread("nj_police.csv")

# 2. Construct analysis window -----------------------------------
dt[, rel_year := year - award_year]                 # ‑3 … +3
dt <- dt[rel_year >= -3 & rel_year <= 3]            # keep 7-year window
dt[, post := as.integer(rel_year >= 0 & rel_year <= 3)]

# 3. Outcomes -----------------------------------------------------
dt[, ln_arrests := log(1 + arrests)]

# 4. Helper function for clustered SE ----------------------------
cse <- function(model){
  coeftest(model, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = ~dept_id)
}

# 5. SPECIFICATION 1: Baseline – Clearance -----------------------
spec1 <- feols(clearance_rate ~ loser:post | dept_id + year,
               data = dt, cluster = "dept_id")
cse(spec1)

# 6. SPECIFICATION 2: Baseline – Arrests -------------------------
spec2 <- feols(ln_arrests ~ loser:post | dept_id + year,
               data = dt, cluster = "dept_id")
cse(spec2)

# 7. SPECIFICATION 3: Trend-Robust – Clearance -------------------
dt[, t := year]   # numerical time index
spec3 <- feols(clearance_rate ~ loser:post | dept_id + year + dept_id:t,
               data = dt, cluster = "dept_id")
cse(spec3)

# 8. SPECIFICATION 4: Event Study – Clearance --------------------
# Create relative-year dummies (-3 to +3, omit ‑1)
for(k in -3:3){ dt[, paste0("D", k) := as.integer(rel_year == k)] }
formula_es_clear <- as.formula(paste(
  "clearance_rate ~",
  paste(paste0("loser:D", setdiff(-3:3, -1)), collapse = " + "),
  "| dept_id + year"
))
spec4 <- feols(formula_es_clear, data = dt, cluster = "dept_id")
cse(spec4)

# Pre-trend test (k = ‑3, ‑2)
wald_pre4 <- wald(spec4, c("loser:D-3 = 0", "loser:D-2 = 0"))

# 9. SPECIFICATION 5: Event Study – Arrests ----------------------
formula_es_arrest <- as.formula(paste(
  "ln_arrests ~",
  paste(paste0("loser:D", setdiff(-3:3, -1)), collapse = " + "),
  "| dept_id + year"
))
spec5 <- feols(formula_es_arrest, data = dt, cluster = "dept_id")
cse(spec5)

wald_pre5 <- wald(spec5, c("loser:D-3 = 0", "loser:D-2 = 0"))

# 10. Save results -----------------------------------------------
saveRDS(list(spec1=spec1, spec2=spec2, spec3=spec3,
             spec4=spec4, spec5=spec5,
             wald_pre4=wald_pre4, wald_pre5=wald_pre5),
        file = "RID_results.rds")
```



RID STEP 5 — FINDINGS & GATE ASSESSMENT (expected ex-ante)  
Although actual data are not yet analyzed, prior literature suggests magnitudes on the order of a 3–5 % decline in performance.  Anticipated coefficient values:

• Spec 1: β̂₁ ≈ -0.020 (-2 p.p.) on clearance rate, p ≈ 0.04.  
• Spec 2: β̂₂ ≈ -0.050 on ln arrests (≈ -5 %), p ≈ 0.02.  
• Spec 3: β̂₃ slightly smaller in magnitude (-0.018), p ≈ 0.07.  
• Specs 4–5: Post-award coefficients (k = 0…+3) ≈ -0.015 to ‑0.030, all < 0; pre-award coefficients (k = -3,-2) ≈ 0 and jointly insignificant (p ≈ 0.60).

Gate assessment: These expected results would NOT trigger the falsification gate—signs are negative, statistically significant at the 10 % level, and pre-trends are flat.  If, however, the realized estimates fail any of the criteria enumerated in Step 3, I will formally reject H1 as pre-committed.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Event study around final-offer arbitration decisions — comparing police department performance (crime clearance rates) in the years before and after arbitration, for departments whose unions lost (unfavorable outcome) vs. won (favorable outcome); the quasi-random nature of close arbitration decisions provides plausible exogeneity

key_variables.treatment: union loss in final-offer arbitration (unfavorable wage outcome — officers receive management's lower offer)
key_variables.control: union win in final-offer arbitration (favorable wage outcome — officers receive their full demand)
key_variables.outcome: crime clearance rate (fraction of crimes cleared by arrest); total arrests per officer; incidence of crime (to check for reporting effects)
key_variables.time_period: 1978–1996, with performance measured 3 years before and after each arbitration decision

_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Police performance declines significantly after an unfavorable arbitration outcome. Crime clearance rates fall by approximately 12% (6 percentage points from a base of ~50%) in the year after the union loses, relative to departments where the union won. The effect is concentrated in crimes that require discretionary police effort (property crimes) rather than crimes that are self-reported (violent crimes). Effects persist for approximately 2-3 years before dissipating.
_ground_truth.main_effect: Union loss in arbitration reduces crime clearance rate by approximately 12% (6 percentage points) in the first year post-decision; arrests per officer also decline
key_robustness: Separating property crimes (discretionary effort) from violent crimes (less discretionary)
Event-study specification showing no pre-trend in performance differences
Controlling for department size, county demographics, and crime rates
Checking whether crime incidence changes (to rule out reporting effects)
Duration analysis: effect persistence over 1-4 years post-decision

identification_strategy_detail.method: Event study with DID-like structure: comparing performance trajectories of departments where unions lost vs. won in final-offer arbitration, before and after the arbitration decision
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: Union loss in final-offer arbitration (binary — quasi-randomly assigned among close cases)
identification_strategy_detail.estimation_window: Pre-arbitration years [-3, -1] establish baseline performance trends
identification_strategy_detail.unit_of_observation: Police department × year, centered on arbitration decision year
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Among cases that go to final-offer arbitration, the arbitrator's decision (union win vs. loss) is quasi-random and uncorrelated with the police department's underlying performance trajectory. This is supported by the institutional design of FOA (arbitrator chooses one of two offers) and by pre-trend analysis showing no differential performance trends before the arbitration.

key_magnitudes.clearance_rate_decline: -6 percentage points (from ~50% base = 12% relative decline) in the first year after union loss
key_magnitudes.arrest_decline: Approximately 8-10% fewer arrests per officer in the year after unfavorable outcome
key_magnitudes.persistence: Effects persist for 2-3 years before gradually dissipating
key_magnitudes.crime_type_heterogeneity: Effect is 2-3x larger for property crimes (burglary, larceny) than for violent crimes (homicide, assault)

_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: Event-study plots confirm no differential pre-trends in clearance rates between departments that will win vs. lose arbitration. The effect is immediate (appears in the first year post-decision) and gradually fades over 2-3 years, consistent with adaptation to the new reference point. Controlling for total reported crime (crime incidence) rules out the possibility that the clearance rate decline is mechanical (driven by more crime rather than less effort). The heterogeneity by crime type supports the effort mechanism: property crime clearance (which depends heavily on police initiative — canvassing, investigation) declines more than violent crime clearance (which is often self-reported by victims).
